lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you drew a design on screen. What does CAD stand for? (Computer-aided design.) Today: how a design on a screen becomes a real object, cut or printed by a machine.
CAD lets designers draw in 2D and 3D: accurate to a fraction of a millimetre, quick to change and easy to share. In 3D CAD you pull a flat sketch up into a solid, then add holes and rounded edges.
CAM (computer-aided manufacture): the computer drives a machine. The design is saved as a file: lines for a laser cutter, or a 3D model for a printer. The machine follows it exactly, again and again.

A laser cutter's beam cuts or engraves flat sheets: plywood, card or acrylic. Lines of one colour are cut through; others are only engraved. The beam burns away a thin line, the kerf. Never leave it running alone.
A 3D printer melts plastic filament and builds the object layer by layer, often 0.2 mm at a time. A model 30 mm tall needs 30 ÷ 0.2 = 150 layers. Its nozzle is about 200 °C.

Additive making builds material up, like a 3D printer. Subtractive making cuts it away, like a laser cutter, a CNC router or a drill. Additive wastes less material; subtractive is often quicker for flat parts.
Worked example: a laser cuts round a 60 mm square. The cut is 4 × 60 = 240 mm long. At 10 mm a second, it takes 240 ÷ 10 = 24 seconds. A thin kerf, about 0.2 mm, is burned away all the way round.
Try it in the world: build your design block by block, layer by layer, like a 3D printer. In LIFE, Real Builder lays a wall course by course in the same way. Next: electronic circuits.

exercises.hint: It is CAD's partner, and its M is about making.
exercises.explain: CAM: computer-aided manufacture, a computer driving a machine.

exercises.prompt: A model is 24 mm tall, printed in layers 0.2 mm thick. How many layers is that?
exercises.hint: Divide the height by one layer's thickness.

exercises.prompt: A 3D printer is an example of additive making.
exercises.hint: Does it add material or take it away?
exercises.explain: True: it adds material, layer by layer.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: additive or subtractive making?
items: building a pot from clay coils
exercises.hint: Is material built up, or cut away?
exercises.explain: Additive: 3D printing, coil pots. Subtractive: laser cutting, drilling, CNC routing.

exercises.prompt: Match each tool to its job.
exercises.hint: Which one designs, and which three make?
exercises.explain: Laser cutter: flat sheets. 3D printer: layer by layer. CNC router: thick blocks. CAD: designs on screen.

exercises.prompt: Label the 3D printer: tap a word, then its number.
exercises.hint: Follow the plastic from where it is stored to where the model grows.
exercises.explain: The spool holds the filament, which feeds the hot nozzle; the layers build up on the bed.

exercises.prompt: A print has 150 layers, and each takes 12 seconds. How many minutes does it take?
exercises.hint: Find the seconds for all the layers, then divide by 60.

exercises.prompt: Why are CAD designs easy to share?
choices: they are files that can be sent and copied
exercises.hint: Where does a CAD design live?
exercises.explain: A CAD design is a file: it can be emailed, copied and changed by a team.

exercises.prompt: The kerf is the thin line of material that the laser burns away.
exercises.hint: What happens to the material right under the beam?
exercises.explain: True: the kerf is the width the beam burns away.

exercises.prompt: Put screen to object in order.
items: the machine cuts or prints it
save the file for the machine
exercises.explain: Sketch, CAD, check on screen, save the file, then the machine makes it.

exercises.prompt: Part of a model hangs out in the air. What does the 3D printer need?
exercises.hint: Can plastic be printed onto nothing?
exercises.explain: Supports underneath hold up the part that hangs out while it prints; they are broken off after.

exercises.prompt: A laser cuts round a 50 mm by 30 mm rectangle at 8 mm a second. How many seconds does the cut take?
exercises.hint: The cut goes all the way round: find the perimeter first.

exercises.prompt: What is the best reason to use CAM for 500 key rings?
choices: every one comes out the same, quickly
exercises.hint: Think about many copies of one design.
exercises.explain: CAM repeats the design exactly and quickly, 500 times.

exercises.prompt: A 3D printer's nozzle is cool enough to touch while it prints.
exercises.hint: What does it do to the plastic?
exercises.explain: False: it melts plastic, at about 200 °C, so never touch it.

exercises.prompt: A sheet is cut into 6 equal strips with 5 straight cuts. Each cut burns a kerf of 0.3 mm. How much width is lost, in mm?
exercises.hint: Multiply the cuts by the width each one burns away.

exercises.prompt: Which usually wastes less material: additive or subtractive making?
exercises.hint: Which one only puts material where the object needs it?
exercises.explain: Additive: it builds only what the design needs, while cutting leaves offcuts.

exercises.hint: Is it flat, from a sheet, or a 3D shape?
exercises.explain: Laser cutter: the key ring, the box net, the engraved sign. 3D printer: the vase, the chess piece.
